title: Validation and the classic attacks
summary: The full validation checklist, and the real attacks it stops: alg=none, algorithm confusion, weak secrets, missing exp and aud checks, and token theft.

steps.title: The validation checklist
body: A signature check alone is not validation. Before trusting any claim in a JWT, an API must check **all** of these:
1. **Shape**: three base64url parts that decode to JSON.
2. **Algorithm**: the header's `alg` is on *your* allow-list for this key. The server decides the algorithm; the token only gets to agree.
3. **Signature**: verified with the key you trust for that issuer.
4. **`exp`**: present, and `now < exp + skew`.
5. **`nbf`**: if present, `now >= nbf - skew`.
6. **`iss`**: exactly the issuer you trust.
7. **`aud`**: contains *your* API's identifier.
8. Only then: read `sub`, roles and scopes and make authorization decisions.
Every item exists because real systems skipped it and were broken. The next cards are the hall of shame.

steps.prompt: Arrange the validation steps in a safe order.
lines: split into three parts and decode the header
reject any alg that is not on the allow-list
check exp and nbf with skew
also: split into three parts and decode the header
reject any alg that is not on the allow-list
check exp and nbf with skew
steps.explain: Algorithm before signature, signature before you believe anything in the payload, and the claims last. The time and iss/aud checks can come in either order.

steps.title: Attacks on the algorithm
body: **`alg: none`.** The JWT spec defines an "unsecured" token with `"alg":"none"` and an empty signature. Early libraries honoured it: an attacker removed the signature, set `alg` to `none`, wrote any claims they liked, and was let in.
```text
eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.
{"alg":"none"}      {"sub":"admin"}       (no signature)

**Algorithm confusion (RS256 → HS256).** A server expects RS256 and has the issuer's *public* key. Its library picks the algorithm from the header. The attacker sends `"alg":"HS256"` and an HMAC computed using **the public key as the HMAC secret**. The public key is public, so anyone can compute that. A naive verifier calls `HMAC(publicKeyBytes, input)`, gets a match, and accepts.
The fix for both is the same: **never let the token choose the algorithm.** Configure each key with the one algorithm it is for, and reject everything else.

**Weak HMAC secrets.** Any single HS256 token is an offline oracle: tools like `hashcat` try billions of candidate secrets per second against it. `"secret"`, `"changeme"` and the company name fall in seconds. Use 32+ random bytes.

steps.prompt: This validator lets the header pick the algorithm. What does it print for an attacker's token?
steps.explain: The attacker controls the header. A validator that reads `alg` from it and obeys has handed the attacker the decision.

steps.prompt: Match each attack to the check that stops it.
pairs: HS256 signed with the RSA public key
binding each key to one algorithm

steps.title: Skipped claim checks, and where tokens live
body: **Not checking `exp`**: a token leaked in a log or a screenshot works forever.

**Not checking `aud`**: your company's identity server issues tokens for many APIs. A token meant for the low-risk *newsletter* API is accepted by the *payments* API, because the signature is valid. `aud` is what says "this token is for me".
**Not checking `iss`**: a token from a different tenant, or the staging identity server, is accepted.
**Where should a browser app keep its token?**
| Storage | XSS can steal it? | CSRF risk? |
| `localStorage` / `sessionStorage` | **Yes**: any script on the page can read it and send it anywhere | No |
| JavaScript memory only | Harder (lost on refresh), still usable by injected script while the page runs | No |
| `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookie | Can't be *read*; injected script can still make requests while the page is open | Yes, so add CSRF defences |

For browser apps the current best practice is the **Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)** pattern: the browser holds only an `HttpOnly` session cookie for its own backend, and that backend keeps the access and refresh tokens server-side and attaches them to API calls. Tokens never reach JavaScript.

steps.prompt: A single-page app stores its access token in `localStorage`. An attacker finds an XSS bug in a comment field. What is the worst consequence?
options: Script in the comment reads the token and sends it to the attacker, who uses it from their own machine until it expires
Nothing, because the token is signed
The attacker learns the signing key
Only the attacker's own account is affected
steps.explain: A signed token is a bearer credential: whoever holds it is the user. `localStorage` is readable by every script on the origin, so XSS turns into token theft. Short lifetimes and the BFF pattern limit the damage.

steps.title: Fix the vulnerable validator
prompt: This validator went to production. It has **four** security bugs:
2. It would accept any algorithm other than `none` too, as long as an HMAC matches. Allow only `HS256` (return `"bad_alg"` for anything else).
3. It compares signatures with `!=`, which is not constant-time. Use `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals` on the decoded bytes.
4. It never checks `exp`. Return `"expired"` when `exp` is missing or `now >= exp` (no skew in this exercise).
Also return `"malformed"` when the token doesn't have three parts. Keep the other return values (`"ok"`, `"bad_signature"`).
Check in this order: three parts, then the algorithm, then the signature, and only then `exp`. A tampered token is `"bad_signature"` even if its payload has no `exp`.

string Validate(string token, byte[] secret, long now)

steps.title: A complete validator
prompt: Write `string Validate(string token, byte[] secret, string issuer, string audience, long now)` that runs the whole checklist with a fixed **60-second skew** and returns the **first** problem it finds:
| `"malformed"` | not three parts, undecodable, or not JSON |

Check in the order of the table: the payload's claims are only read once the signature is good, so a tampered token is `"bad_signature"` even if its payload has no `exp`. Never throw. Bring your own `B64Url` / `FromB64Url`. The tests import `System.Security.Cryptography` and `System.Text.Json`.
starter: string Validate(string token, byte[] secret, string issuer, string audience, long now)
solution: case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
string Validate(string token, byte[] secret, string issuer, string audience, long now)
if (!header.RootElement.TryGetProperty("alg", out var alg) || alg.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.String || alg.GetString() != "HS256")
if (!root.TryGetProperty("exp", out var exp) || exp.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Number) return "malformed";
if (root.TryGetProperty("nbf", out var nbf) && now < nbf.GetInt64() - Skew) return "not_yet_valid";
if (!root.TryGetProperty("iss", out var iss) || iss.GetString() != issuer) return "bad_issuer";
JsonValueKind.Array => aud.EnumerateArray().Any(a => a.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String && a.GetString() == audience),
catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException or InvalidOperationException)
hints: Structure it as a series of early returns inside one `try`, with `catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException or InvalidOperationException) { return "malformed"; }`.
Reuse your `HasAudience` logic for the array case.
template: Dojo.Eq("a good token -> ok", "ok", Validate(Good(), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("not a JWT -> malformed", "malformed", Validate("hello", S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("undecodable parts -> malformed", "malformed", Validate("@@@.@@@.@@@", S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("alg none -> bad_alg", "bad_alg", Validate("eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.", S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("alg RS256 -> bad_alg", "bad_alg", Validate(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"alg\":\"RS256\"}", "{\"exp\":1700000900}", S), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("wrong secret -> bad_signature", "bad_signature", Validate(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"exp\":1700000900}", new byte[32]), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("tampered payload -> bad_signature", "bad_signature", Validate(DojoJwt.Tamper(Good()), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("no exp -> malformed", "malformed", Validate(Tok("{\"iss\":\"https://auth.dojo\",\"aud\":\"tasks-api\"}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("exp as a string -> malformed", "malformed", Validate(Tok("{\"exp\":\"tomorrow\"}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("30s after exp (inside skew) -> ok", "ok", Validate(Good(), S, Iss, Aud, 1700000930));
Dojo.Eq("60s after exp -> expired", "expired", Validate(Good(), S, Iss, Aud, 1700000960));
Dojo.Eq("nbf in the future -> not_yet_valid", "not_yet_valid", Validate(Good(), S, Iss, Aud, 1699999900));
Dojo.Eq("nbf just inside skew -> ok", "ok", Validate(Good(), S, Iss, Aud, 1699999950));
Dojo.Eq("wrong issuer -> bad_issuer", "bad_issuer", Validate(Tok("{\"iss\":\"https://evil.dojo\",\"aud\":\"tasks-api\",\"exp\":1700000900}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("no issuer -> bad_issuer", "bad_issuer", Validate(Tok("{\"aud\":\"tasks-api\",\"exp\":1700000900}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("wrong audience -> bad_audience", "bad_audience", Validate(Tok("{\"iss\":\"https://auth.dojo\",\"aud\":\"billing-api\",\"exp\":1700000900}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("audience array containing ours -> ok", "ok", Validate(Tok("{\"iss\":\"https://auth.dojo\",\"aud\":[\"billing-api\",\"tasks-api\"],\"exp\":1700000900}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("no audience -> bad_audience", "bad_audience", Validate(Tok("{\"iss\":\"https://auth.dojo\",\"exp\":1700000900}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
Dojo.Eq("an expired token for another API reports expired first", "expired", Validate(Tok("{\"iss\":\"x\",\"aud\":\"y\",\"exp\":1}"), S, Iss, Aud, Now));
